questions.heading: Compare Computed Floats With a Tolerance You Chose, Never With ==
questions.stem: A test asserts that a crew plan's discounted cost == 4813.27. After a teammate rewrites the discounting loop, the function returns 4813.270000000001, and both versions of the formula are correct. How should the test compare the two numbers?

options.text: Round both sides to two decimals before comparing, since costs are reported in cents
options.says: Rounding can turn a tiny difference into a whole cent when a value sits near a rounding boundary.

options.text: Restore the old loop, since a rewrite should return exactly the bits the old one did
options.says: Both formulas are right; floats round at different steps, so equal formulas can differ in the last digit.

options.text: Compare with pytest.approx and a $k tolerance, since float sums depend on their order
options.says: Right: a tolerance says how close counts as equal; approx's default rel=1e-6 is about $0.005k here.

options.text: Cast both sides to int before comparing, since GridCap stores its money in whole $k
options.says: Integer money is exact, but a discounted cost is a float; truncating it throws away the part being tested.

questions.heading: A Fixture Builds an Input Once and Hands It to Every Test That Names It
questions.stem: A fixture declared as @pytest.fixture, with no scope argument, loads a portfolio in two seconds. Thirty tests in one file name it as a parameter. How many times does pytest call the fixture in one run of that file?

options.text: Once, since pytest caches a fixture's result after the first test asks for it
options.says: Keeping one result for the whole file is what scope='module' asks for; the default does not.

options.text: Once for each test, since function scope rebuilds the fixture for every test that asks
options.says: Right: the default scope is the function, so each test gets its own build.

options.text: Once per test file, since module scope is what a fixture gets unless told otherwise
options.says: Sharing within a file is scope='module', which this fixture does not declare.

options.text: Never, since a fixture runs only when a test calls the fixture function itself
options.says: A test asks for a fixture by naming it as a parameter, and pytest calls the fixture.

questions.heading: Parametrize Turns a Table of Cases Into One Test per Row, and Each Case Breaks One Rule
questions.stem: A parametrized case for an outage validator is a request with negative hours and an unknown crew, and its test only asserts that the request is rejected. Someone deletes the negative-hours check by mistake. What does that test do now?

options.text: It fails, since the request no longer breaks the rule the case was named for
options.says: The test only asks whether the request is rejected, and the unknown crew still rejects it.

options.text: It fails, since parametrize runs each of the validator's rules on its own
options.says: Parametrize runs the test once per case, not once per rule of the code under test.

options.text: It errors, since a case that breaks two rules cannot be given to parametrize
options.says: Parametrize accepts any values; nothing checks how many rules a case breaks.

options.text: It still passes, since the request still breaks another of the validator's rules
options.says: Right: a case that breaks two rules hides a broken check, which is why each case breaks one rule.
